verdicts.trueWording: far harder to "humanize"
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the Introduction (with 'humanize' in scare quotes). §4.2 confirms 93.9% macro-F1 on style-edited stories vs 95.5% unedited, a 1.6-point drop. One precision caveat: the rewriting is LAMP span-level artifact removal performed by Gemini itself using 25 few-shot examples from professional writers on 278 Gemini stories — not rewriting by professionals, so 'professional-style rewriting' is a loose gloss.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "professional-style rewriting" — the edit was Gemini's own LAMP span-level artifact removal, not rewriting by professionals.

verdicts.trueWording: delves (r=28.0), showcasing (r=10.2), underscores (r=10.9); 66% verbs, 16% adjectives
verdicts.note: No quote supplied. Kobak et al. give delves r=28.0 and showcasing r=10.2 exactly, and 'hundreds of words have abruptly increased their frequency after ChatGPT became available'. The POS split is real but narrower than stated: 'Out of all 319 excess style words in 2024, 66% were verbs and 16% were adjectives' — style words, not all excess words. 'intricate' is the paper's own example of a style word; 'pivotal', 'realm' and 'meticulously' appear in the paper only as words identified by cited work (Liang et al. 2024b; Gray 2024) and in illustrative AI-style sentences, not in Kobak's own headline excess list.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the 66%-verbs/16%-adjectives split holds only of the 319 excess STYLE words, and pivotal, realm and meticulously are not in Kobak's own excess list.

verdicts.trueWording: lexical overrepresentation remains a feature of current iterations of ChatGPT
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in §7 (sentence-internal, so lowercase 'lexical'). Appendix A's table of 21 focal words contains every word named in the claim: delve/delves/delved/delving, showcasing, underscores, intricate, garnered, boasts, groundbreaking, realm, aligns. §4 and Appendix B confirm the words are not overrepresented in pre-LLM corpora (arXiv, LCC, PubMed, Wikipedia). One hedge: the paper reports 'mixed evidence' for RLHF — 'the model testing is consistent with RLHF playing a role', not a demonstrated source.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "consistent with RLHF as the source" — the paper reports mixed evidence, only that testing is "consistent with RLHF playing a role", not a demonstrated source.

verdicts.trueWording: wary of the word "delve"
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the Introduction ('participants became wary of the word "delve" in the first sentence of an abstract') and echoed in §6 as 'Wariness about the word "delve"'. Caveat on the second half: the paper's line about judging on words rather than content is a speculation about rushed, underpaid RLHF evaluators — 'Rushed human evaluators might base their evaluations on the presence of particular words rather than on content' — not a finding about readers generally.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "readers may judge a text on those words rather than its content" — the paper says this of rushed RLHF evaluators, not of readers generally.

verdicts.trueWording: tend to fall short in terms of novelty, surprise and diversity
verdicts.note: Quote matches word for word. The abstract also confirms the design (60 LLMs, 60 people, five-sentence cue-word task) and the comparison class ('average human writers'). Caveat: the p-value range (p<0.05 to p<0.0001) does not appear anywhere on this abstract-only page, and 'diversity' is not broken out into lexical vs semantic.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the p<0.05-to-p<0.0001 range and the lexical-vs-semantic split of diversity appear nowhere on the cited abstract page.

verdicts.trueWording: LLMs generate stylistically complex stories, but tend to fall short
verdicts.note: The quoted wording is not on the page. The core proposition — more complex yet less creative — is supported: the abstract says LLMs 'generate stylistically complex stories, but tend to fall short in terms of novelty, surprise and diversity,' and lists linguistic complexity among the measured dimensions. The specific verbosity evidence (unique words, dependency path length, noun and adjective counts) is absent; searches for 'verbos', 'unique words', 'dependency', 'noun', 'adjective' returned zero hits.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the verbosity evidence (more unique words, longer dependency paths, more nouns and adjectives) is absent from the page — zero hits on every search term.

verdicts.trueWording: collectively a narrower scope of novel content is produced
verdicts.note: Quote matches word for word, and the page is confirmed as Doshi & Hauser (Science Advances, GPT-4 ideas). Concentration of individual gains among low-creativity writers is supported ('especially among less creative writers'). IMPORTANT CORRECTION: 10.7% is misdescribed. The paper says the similarity increase 'represents 10.7% and 8.9% of the total range' of similarity scores (an 8.10-point range) — not that stories were 10.7% more similar to one another. Separately, 5.2% more similar to the AI ideas is the ONE-idea condition; the five-idea condition is 5.0%. A different 10.7% elsewhere on the page refers to novelty gains for low-DAT writers, which may be the source of the conflation.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "stories 10.7% more similar to one another" — the paper's 10.7% is a share of the similarity score's total range, not a similarity increase, and 5.2% is the one-idea condition alone.

verdicts.trueWording: "informationally dense, noun-heavy style"
verdicts.note: Quote appears verbatim twice. Figures confirmed: nominalizations 'at 1.5 to 2 times the rate of humans' generally, and for GPT-4o specifically ''that' clauses as subject 2.6 times as often (d=0.77), nominalizations 2.1 times as often (d=1.23), and phrasal coordination 1.9 times as often (d=0.81)'. Two glosses: the 2.6x and 1.9x figures are GPT-4o-specific, not all instruction-tuned models; and 'academic' is the claim's word, not the paper's, though the paper does attribute the style to instruction tuning across a diverse array of genres.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the 2.6x "that"-clause and 1.9x phrasal-coordination rates are GPT-4o-specific, not all instruction-tuned models, and "academic" is not the paper's word.

verdicts.trueWording: "a word like unspoken occurs in about 15% of LLM-generated responses"
verdicts.note: No quote supplied, but both halves are explicit in Section 5.3: 'Figure 6 shows how a word like unspoken occurs in about 15% of LLM-generated responses. Similarly phrases such as weight of, sense of, mix of occur very rarely or not at all in original seed paragraphs... while they occur frequently in LLM-generated responses.' One imprecision: the paper reserves 'syntactic templates' for its part-of-speech n-gram analysis (Table 8) and files these three phrases under recurrent awkward words/phrases; the claim merges the two.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "templates" — the paper files "sense of / weight of / mix of" under recurrent awkward words and phrases, reserving "syntactic templates" for its POS n-gram analysis.

verdicts.trueWording: "LLM-generated stories lead to 7–9 higher drop ratio than human-written ones"
verdicts.note: No quote supplied. Figure confirmed in Section 5 (the page literally reads '7–9 higher drop ratio', the multiplication sign apparently lost in the HTML build). Mechanism supported: 'a high drop ratio indicates that the Sui Generis score decreases immediately after the peak at position i, without progressively unraveling the surprising plot,' associated with 'abrupt resolutions that leave key suspenseful plot elements unresolved.' Slight tension in the claim's gloss: the paper's drop measures a surprising element being dropped or hastily closed off, sometimes left unresolved, rather than strictly 'resolved'.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "resolved immediately after it peaks" — the paper's drop measures an element dropped or hastily closed off, sometimes left unresolved, not strictly resolved.

verdicts.trueWording: "a substantial advancement (i.e., early occurrence) of TP4 and TP5"
verdicts.note: The quote 'higher levels of suspense' IS verbatim ('human-written stories consistently exhibit higher levels of suspense'), as is the widening gap ('the gap begins to enlarge as the plot progresses from the midpoint (0.5 relative position) towards the end'). Downgraded from VERBATIM because the claim's magnitude is unsourced: the strings '10%' and '15%' appear nowhere in the paper, and the earlier arrival of Major Setback (TP4) and Climax (TP5) is reported only qualitatively plus a violin plot (Figure 2) with no numeric positions. The '10–15% earlier' figure appears to be eyeballed from that figure.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "about 10–15% earlier" — the strings 10% and 15% appear nowhere in the paper; the advancement of TP4/TP5 is reported only qualitatively and in a violin plot.

verdicts.trueWording: less conflict-driven social dynamics
verdicts.note: arXiv 2510.18932v1, Nonaka & Perry. Quote verbatim. Table 1 in the raw HTML confirms density 0.338–0.470 vs human 0.182, clustering 0.623–0.766 vs 0.485, human mean edge weight −0.061 ('the only negative average edge weight'). ONE CORRECTION: the LLM edge-weight range is 0.235–0.659 (GPT-4o Mini = 0.235), not 0.236–0.659. Human corpus is confirmed science fiction (Project Gutenberg, genre-filtered, n=168). 'Far less variability' is supported by the paper's framing — 'LLMs have connectivity measure scores that cluster closely, while human-written stories are dispersed' — though per-metric SDs are mixed (human density SD 0.056 is actually lower than every model's).
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the LLM edge-weight floor is 0.235 (GPT-4o Mini), not 0.236, and "far less variability" is not borne out per-metric — human density SD (0.056) is lower than every model's.

verdicts.trueWording: roughly twice the human baseline
verdicts.note: arXiv 2609.02482v1, Rohrbacher, Nieth, Salin, Eskofier & Mahlberg. Verbatim: 'Whereas human-authored fiction shows normalized frequencies of around 0.19 in both languages, all four models exceed this level, with GPT 4.1 reaching around 0.47 in English and 0.38 in German, roughly twice the human baseline.' CAVEAT on the second half: the action-space deficit is not universal — 'GPT 4.1 is the only model that remains close to or above the human baseline'; Gemma 3, Mistral 3.2 and LlaMA 3.3 fall below it. The abstract's own framing does support the substitution claim: humans 'predominantly employ action space ... whereas LLMs systematically overproduce perceived space, emphasizing atmosphere and affect.'
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the action-space deficit is not universal — GPT 4.1 stays close to or above the human baseline; only Gemma 3, Mistral 3.2 and LlaMA 3.3 fall below it.

verdicts.trueWording: GPT-4 receives predominantly scores of 0/1, while Pron receives mostly 2/3
verdicts.note: arXiv 2407.01119v2, Marco, Gonzalo, Mateo & Ramón del Castillo. Quote verbatim ('In all dimensions, GPT-4 receives predominantly scores of 0/1, while Pron receives mostly 2/3.'). Verified: 'We recruited six literary experts'; the task is 600-word synopses of imaginary movie titles, so 'synopses' is correct; 'Pron's creativity score is particularly high (average of 1.94)'; 'GPT-4 scores are particularly low in style originality (0.36 in Spanish and 0.63 in English), where Pron gets 1.70'. CAVEAT: the two GPT-4 creativity figures (0.97 English, 0.88 Spanish) do NOT appear anywhere in the page text — the text says only that Pron's 1.94 'roughly doubles GPT-4 creativity scores in English and Spanish'. Those values presumably sit inside Figure 1, which is an image and not machine-readable, so they are consistent with but not confirmable from the page.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the GPT-4 creativity figures 0.97 (English) and 0.88 (Spanish) do not appear anywhere in the page text; they sit inside a non-machine-readable figure.

verdicts.trueWording: Humans retain an edge in creativity
verdicts.note: Quote is word for word in the abstract on the ACL Anthology landing page. That page carries the abstract only — none of the numbers are on it — so I additionally pulled the paper PDF (aclanthology.org/2023.findings-emnlp.966.pdf), Table 2, which confirms every figure: chatgpt-gpt4 overall 80.2±7.3 vs human 70.1±17.4; item 7 (epic-genre habitation) 8.1±1.4 vs 4.9±2.1; item 5 (creativity/originality) human 8.0±2 vs 7.6±1; item 10 (dark humor) human 6.4±3.4 vs 6.0±2.8. Human stories were by five different writers. One imprecision: humans also edged GPT-4 on humor (6.4 vs 6.0), so 'led only on originality' is not strictly true, though the claim itself calls humor near-tied.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "humans led only on originality" is not strictly true — humans also edged GPT-4 on humor, 6.4 vs 6.0.

verdicts.trueWording: less variation when compared to human-generated sentences
verdicts.note: Quote is word for word. Same sentence continues: 'the models exhibit a higher frequency of sentence generation within the 10 to 30 token range compared to humans'. Caveat on the STTR pair: Table 2 gives Human 0.491 and six models at 0.452 / 0.424 / 0.460 / 0.457 / 0.461 / 0.466 — 0.424 is Falcon-7B alone, the lowest model, not an LLM-wide value; the LLM range is 0.424-0.466. Direction of the claim ('lexical richness is lower') holds for all six.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: STTR 0.424 is Falcon-7B alone, the lowest model, not an LLM-wide value; the model range is 0.424–0.466.

verdicts.trueWording: Humans exhibit stronger fear and disgust, less joy
verdicts.note: No quotation supplied. Conclusion states: 'Humans tend to exhibit stronger negative emotions (such as fear and disgust) and less joy compared to text generated by LLMs'; 'LLM outputs use more numbers, symbols and auxiliaries ... as well as more pronouns'; 'The sexist bias prevalent in human text is also expressed by LLMs, and even magnified in all of them but' Falcon 7B. Table 9: human male-female pronoun ratio 1.71, exceeded by every model except Falcon 7B, which reduces the bias by 7.5% — the one exception the claim's blanket 'magnify' elides.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the blanket "magnify male-pronoun bias" elides Falcon 7B, the one model that reduces the bias (by 7.5%).

verdicts.trueWording: a broader and flatter distribution
verdicts.note: Quote word for word: human texts 'exhibit greater variability in length, characterized by a broader and flatter distribution. In contrast, AI-generated texts ... are more uniform, clustering closely around the average.' Table 3 confirms all three ranges, but ONLY in the factual-news columns: informal -54.42/-55.99/-72.22%, posemo +114.19/+119.22/+132.96%, certain +152.49/+142.86/+111.00%. The fake-news columns are materially lower (posemo +69.96 to +78.95%, certain +21.43 to +39.11%), so the claim should be scoped to factual news. Source confirmed as Rodrigues, Sturm & Pinheiro, iScience 2026 Feb 12;29(3):114976, European Portuguese.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the 54–72% / 114–133% / 111–152% ranges hold only in the factual-news columns; the fake-news columns are materially lower (posemo +70 to +79%, certain +21 to +39%).

verdicts.trueWording: illogical in hindsight
verdicts.note: Quote is a verbatim annotation tag in the paper PDF. Body: 'as 32% of generations rated by at least one player are deemed illogical upon reading the next utterance' - the claim's '32% of GPT-4 game lines' drops the 'rated by at least one player' qualifier, a mild overstatement. Faction example confirmed: generation 'does not conform to the game's notion of an ultra-liberal character'.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "32% of GPT-4 game lines" drops the paper's "rated by at least one player" qualifier — a mild overstatement.

verdicts.trueWording: preliminary end-to-end experiments revealed these shortcomings, say the authors
verdicts.note: MISATTRIBUTION. The quoted string is verbatim on the page, but it describes the AUTHORS' OWN preliminary experiments: 'Our preliminary experiments with this end-to-end approach revealed suboptimal results. The generated screenplays often suffer from a lack of thematic focus, out-of-character dialogue, and insufficient character development.' The blind evaluation by 'over 20 experienced screenwriters' (professional Chinese television drama screenwriters) produced the Expert Score / 75% win rate, not this defect list. 'Mimicking screenplay style without conciseness or visual language' is also the authors' intro framing: 'outputs that superficially mimic screenplay style but lack the conciseness, visual language, and structural integrity'.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the defect list is misattributed — thematic focus, out-of-character dialogue and thin character development come from the authors' own preliminary experiments, not from the blind screenwriter evaluation.

verdicts.trueWording: some studies identifying trends toward overly positive or uninspired endings
verdicts.note: MISATTRIBUTION. Quote is verbatim but is the authors citing prior literature in the introduction ('with some studies identifying trends toward overly positive or uninspired endings [13]'), not something the expert panel recorded. 'Unconvincing, repetitive, or misaligned with the desired tone or character development' is likewise the authors' framing in the introduction. Only the genre element is genuinely a panel finding: 'experts raised concerns about the degree to which the story aligns with, subverts, or engages with genre conventions'.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: misattributed — "unconvincing, repetitive, tonally misaligned" and "overly positive or uninspired endings" are the authors citing prior literature; only the genre item is an expert-panel finding.

verdicts.trueWording: a 'vibe' that the story felt artificial
verdicts.note: Outlook Respawn, Krishna Goswami, 15 Dec 2025. Quote verbatim. Shrine's Legacy by Positive Concept Games; devs state they 'worked exclusively with human talent for everything from writing to coding' and 'do not endorse generative AI and will never use it'. Page supplies the false-positive frame directly: 'A 2024 Microsoft study found that users can correctly identify AI-generated content only about 62% of the time, suggesting that "gut feelings" about art or dialogue are frequently wrong.' Precision note: the ChatGPT accusation came from one 'belligerent review' saying the narrative was 'made in ChatGPT'; the felt-artificial vibe is from OTHER reviews, so 'because' overstates a single causal chain.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "because the story felt artificial" overstates a single causal chain — the ChatGPT accusation was one belligerent review; the felt-artificial vibe came from other reviews.

verdicts.trueWording: em dash still far outstrips the semi-colon and exclamation mark
verdicts.note: SALT.agency, Sarah Mitchell, January 29, 2026. The supplied quote IS on the page word for word, but it supports a DIFFERENT point (detector unreliability), not the Ngram claim -- so it cannot be cited as evidence for this claim. The Ngram substance is on the page: a 'Google Books Ngram graph comparing the frequencies of the em dash (in blue), semi-colon (red) and exclamation point (green) in books published between 1500 and 2022', plus 'precious little evidence that ChatGPT does use the em dash too frequently; or at least more frequently than the average professional writer' and the training-data argument about professionally edited pre-internet text. CONTRADICTS 'stayed high for centuries': the page states 'the frequency in usage of the em dash does drop away after the mid-'90s' -- what survives is relative dominance, not a flat curve. Re-cut the claim to the dominance wording.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "em dash frequency has stayed high for centuries" is contradicted — the page states usage "does drop away after the mid-'90s"; only relative dominance survives (and the supplied quote supports detector unreliability, a different point).

verdicts.trueWording: a diagnostic signature of how a model was fine-tuned
verdicts.note: Quote exact. Every figure confirmed: 'weighted mean across our sample was 3.23 per 1,000 words (median 3.83; range 0.33-17.12)'; GPT-4.1 unconstrained 10.62; 'twelve models from five providers'; 'Meta's Llama models produce zero'; base-vs-instruct Llama 3.1 8B shows 'a latent tendency exists pre-RLHF, with the direction and magnitude of amplification determined by the fine-tuning procedure'. One loose word: 'envelops' overstates - the human range 0.33-17.12 does not reach the LLM floor of 0.0.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "envelops" overstates — the human range 0.33–17.12 does not reach the LLM floor of 0.0.

verdicts.trueWording: also be attributed to amateurish or unedited writing
verdicts.note: Quote exact (Anne R. Allen quoting Mark Williams at TNPS). New York/1990s supported: 'Because New York publishing taught us to. I first heard the term "em dash" ... in the mid-1990s. I'd scored an in-person critique ... by a real New York editor.' Neurodivergent/ESL supported: 'these are also the "tells" of an autistic or ESL writer.' One gloss: the reported tells are 'the narrative voice was all over the place', 'no emotional engagement', 'improbable similes and superfluous verbiage' - 'flat voice' is the claim's paraphrase, not the article's word.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "flat voice" is the claim's paraphrase; the reported tell is "the narrative voice was all over the place".

verdicts.note: Quote exact, inside a quoted tweet: 'Imagine after being force-fed colonial languages, being forced to speak it better than its owners then being told that no one used basic words like \'delve\' in real life. verdicts.trueWording: probably not overrepresented in the training data
verdicts.note: Quote exact. '21 focal words' exact, and delve/intricate/underscore/realm are all in the Table 2 list. Variety claim exact in substance: 'we do not find evidence that the focal words are especially prevalent in any particular variety of English'; the Nigerian-English hypothesis is named and rejected - 'Our initial analysis of ICE does not support this hypothesis.' One hedge lost in the claim: the paper says only that 'the model testing is consistent with RLHF playing a role', weaker than 'likely post-training'.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "likely post-training" overstates the paper's hedge, that testing is only "consistent with RLHF playing a role".

verdicts.trueWording: reduced detection rates from 100% to 13%
verdicts.note: Quote is a paraphrase, not on the page in any form; the paper reads 'a second-round self-edit prompt ("Elevate the provided text by employing literary language") applied to ChatGPT-3.5 significantly reduced detection rates from 100% to 13%' - no 'up to' on either figure. The abstract figures are right (68% -> 28%: 'still identified up to 68% of fake abstracts ... lowered detection rates to up to 28%') but come from a DIFFERENT prompt, 'employing advanced technical language', so the claim's 'a single \'employ literary language\' self-edit prompt' covering both results is wrong. Same URL caveat as 237: figures are in the full text, not the /abs/ page.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: attributing both results to a single "employ literary language" prompt is wrong — the 68%→28% abstract figures come from a different prompt ("employing advanced technical language"), and the quote's "up to" phrasing is not on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: our recursive paraphrasing method can significantly reduce detection rates
verdicts.note: Quote appears word for word in the abstract, as do watermarking, neural network-based detectors, zero shot classifiers, retrieval-based detectors, and spoofing 'aimed at misclassifying human-written text as AI-generated'. Caveat: the current abstract states the theory only as 'a theoretical framework connecting the AUROC of the best possible detector to the Total Variation distance between human and AI text distributions' — the claim's gloss 'degrades toward random as distributions approach human ones' is the paper's result but is not spelled out in the abstract text now on the page.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "degrades toward random as LLM text distributions approach human ones" is not spelled out in the abstract now on the page, which states only an AUROC/Total-Variation theoretical framework.

verdicts.trueWording: LLM-generated stories pass 3-10X less TTCW tests than stories written by professionals
verdicts.note: Quote appears word for word. Abstract confirms 'TTCW consists of 14 binary tests', 'We recruit 10 creative writers', and 'none of the LLMs positively correlate with the expert assessments'. Caveat: the dimensional gloss is only half supported - the paper states 'all models achieve their highest pass rate on the Fluency dimension' and Table 5 puts Originality lowest, but it does not single out Elaboration as a deficit (Elaboration tracks Flexibility), and it frames the gap as broad rather than concentrated.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the dimensional gloss is only half supported — the paper does not single out Elaboration as a deficit and frames the gap as broad rather than concentrated.
